neutral_facts.value: The accused, a man, was convicted of the murder and rape of a 10-year-old girl. The victim was found dead inside the accused's house with blood stains under the cot. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including the presence of the victim's body in the accused's house, blood stains on the bedsheet and floor, and the absence of any explanation from the accused for how the victim's body arrived at his house. The accused claimed he had gone to a liquor shop, but this was found to be false. The victim's body was discovered by the police, and the medical report indicated sexual assault and strangulation as the cause of death. The trial court convicted the accused and sentenced him to life imprisonment for murder and 10 years for rape, with both sentences to run concurrently. The High Court upheld the conviction but enhanced the sentence to death, which was later overturned by the Supreme Court, restoring the life imprisonment sentence.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the appellant caused the death of a minor girl aged 10 years by strangulating her after committing rape on her. The case was based on circumstantial evidence, and the trial court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to life imprisonment under Section 302 IPC and 10 years imprisonment under Section 376 IPC. The High Court upheld the conviction but enhanced the sentence to death penalty.

quotes.text: The prosecution argued that the appellant caused the death of a minor girl aged 10 years by strangulating her after committing rape on her.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that there was no evidence on record to connect the appellant with the crime. Circumstantial evidence was not sufficient to indicate the appellant's guilt, and the High Court was not justified in enhancing the punishment from life imprisonment to death sentence.

quotes.text: There is no evidence on record to connect the appellant with the crime.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a conviction based on circumstantial evidence must be conclusive, exclude all possible hypotheses except the one to be proved, and form a complete chain of evidence. The court also applied the 'rarest of rare cases' test for the imposition of the death sentence.
